title: Step 3 (extra) – The capture is huge: shorten every packet to 128 bytes
cmd: ls -lh skill4_capture.pcapng; editcap -s 128 skill4_capture.pcapng skill4_capture_128B.pcapng; ls -lh skill4_capture_128B.pcapng
note: The 5-second iPerf3 test ran at ~56 Gbit/s, so the raw capture is 6 GB. editcap keeps only the first 128 bytes of each packet (enough for all headers and complete ICMP packets) – 24 MB.
output:
-rw-------@ 1 divyasaisomana  staff   6.0G Nov 19 15:08 skill4_capture.pcapng
-rw-r--r--@ 1 divyasaisomana  staff    24M Nov 19 15:09 skill4_capture_128B.pcapng

title: Step 3 (extra) – Keep the small capture as skill4_capture.pcapng
cmd: rm skill4_capture.pcapng && mv skill4_capture_128B.pcapng skill4_capture.pcapng; ls -lh skill4_capture.pcapng
note: The 6 GB original is deleted; the 24 MB file is used for the analysis.

title: Step 3 – Apply the display filter: icmp or tcp.port == 5201 or udp.port == 5201 (count)
cmd: tshark -r skill4_capture.pcapng -Y "icmp or tcp.port == 5201 or udp.port == 5201" 2>/dev/null | wc -l
note: Number of ICMP + iPerf3 packets shown by the filter.

title: Step 3 – Display filter: tcp.port == 5201 (iPerf3 traffic, first lines)
note: iPerf3 control and data connection (TCP port 5201) between Computer 2 and Computer 1.

title: Step 4 – Wireshark filter icmp: Echo Request and Echo Reply packets
note: Echo (ping) request and reply pairs are visible. Each reply points back to its request.

title: Step 4 – Count Echo Requests and Echo Replies
cmd: echo -n "Echo requests: "; tshark -r skill4_capture.pcapng -Y "icmp.type == 8" 2>/dev/null | wc -l; echo -n "Echo replies : "; tshark -r skill4_capture.pcapng -Y "icmp.type == 0" 2>/dev/null | wc -l
note: 200 pings were sent in each of the two baseline runs (400 in total) – every request has a reply.

title: Step 4 – Time difference between request and reply (icmp.resptime)
cmd: tshark -r skill4_capture.pcapng -Y "icmp.type == 0" -T fields -e frame.number -e icmp.seq -e icmp.resptime 2>/dev/null | head -15
note: Wireshark's 'Response time' field (ms) for each Echo Reply – the same value as the ping RTT.

title: Latency percentiles of the baseline RTT file
note: Mean, p50, p90, p95, p99 and max of the 200 RTT samples – tail percentiles show spikes that the average hides.

title: Wireshark RTT statistics for all echo replies (mean of icmp.resptime)
note: Capture-based average and maximum response time.
